1t is ninety-four years now
since the jubilant Wings raised
this shout throughout the coun-
try signifying the bolt of the
Pine Tree State from Van
Buren's Democrats to the party
of William Henry Harrison.
That happened in the year 1910,
the date of the famous hard
cider-log cabin" campaign, and
every two years since we have
been reminded "as Maine goes
so goes the nation"


1t isn't exactly true and it is
not borne out by the cold fig
ures, but we hear it neverthe-
less, and are hearing it now as
September 10 draws near, the
day on which Maine will elect
a United States Senator, a gov
ernor and its quota of three
Representatives to Congress.


The Democrats had their
chance in 1882, for the first
time in the memory of living
man, to seize upon the State
prophecy and to see it fulfilled
beyond all expectations in the
Presidential election. The
chances are that this year the
Republicans will get some COM
fort from the returns.


The Democrats. especially the
urbane James AloySiuS Farley,
concede nothing, but precedent
is against them. For them to
retain the governorship and two
seats in Congress would be an
amazing victory. And they
could count it as a moral tri-
umph if only they lose every
thing but keep the Republican
margin down to a negligible
figure.


This is an off-year and in
every off-year Congressional
elections in the past sixty, the
party of the President has lost
seats in Congress. The number
varies with times and conditions.
For example the oil scandals
cost the Harding adminiStra-
ton Seventy-seven seats in 1922,
whereas prosperity came along
in 1925, the Coolidge admins
tration got by with but nine
defeats.


A survey of the history of
Maine elections made by Co
lumbia University in 1880
showed that in off years the
state is a poor barometer of the
Congressional lineup, being
wrong on an average of twelve
seats. The record for PreSiden-
tial years is somewhat better,
for in seventeen out of the past
twenty-four Presidential elec-
tionS, the party which elected
the governor of Maine in Sep
tember elected the new Presi-
dent of the United States two
months later.

St. Paul, Feb. 19—To be underweight after 40 years of age increases the prospect of living to a ripe old age.

At all ages of maturity those who are overweight provide the largest target for death.

These conclusions arrived at on the basis of a careful study quoted by the United States Public Health Service are cited and endorsed in a bulletin issued today by the Public Health Education Committee of the Minnesota State Medical Association.

The figures provided by this study constitute an overwhelming argument for proceeding with discretion and an eye to the scales in adult life, in the opinion of this committee.

Deaths from organic heart disease among those over 40 years of age are found by the Public Health Service to be 253 per 100,000 for persons 50 pounds or more over average weight. The figure is 213 for those of more normal weight and it is reduced to 161 for those who are 15 pounds or more underweight. Deaths from any specific cause are highest for overweight men between the ages of 50 and 70 years suffering from heart disorders.

Appendicitis and kindred diseases are also shown to take the highest mortality among those who are overweight of all ages, likewise, nephritis and Bright's disease, which also, deaths from these figures show, take their heaviest toll among men of 50 pounds or more overweight of all ages. Similarly, diabetes death rates are highest among them, also cerebral or brain hemorrhage and apoplexy.

At the same time, the physicians emphasize the point that the relation of weight to deaths in youth may be a different story. Underweight is found to be an important factor in excess mortality in the case of tuberculosis, for instance. In general death is more partial in youth to those who weigh less than they should.

RALEIGH, Jan. 1.—The department of revenue is getting ready to tighten up on the collection of the state income tax, it was learned today from Commissioner of Revenue A. J. Maxwell. For while the income tax is not due until March 15, district meetings of the field deputy collectors are already being held in which detailed instructions in the income tax law and how to collect it and check up on collections, are being given. The suggestions, it was said, were outlined at meeting of the British and American naval delegations yesterday. The meeting was described as a rehearsal of possible bases for a British-American accord in every contingency—namely, with or without an international treaty of limitation.

Norman H. Davis, chief American delegate, was believed to have reported the suggestions to the State Department in Washington. It was understood on reliable authority that he made no commitment to the British.

It was said specifically that cooperation was envisaged and in no sense an alliance.

Britain was said to have outlined proposals as follows:

1. The British government is unequivocally in favor of maintaining the present agreement regarding Notifications and naval bases in the Pacific.

2. The British asked that the United States limit its battleships in future to 26,000 tons, with 12-inch guns, and cruisers to 7,500 tons with 6-inch guns, the limitation to be applicable only to future construction.

(The largest American battleships now are around 32,500 and the largest guns 16-inch. The big cruisers are 10,000 tons with 8-inch guns).

3. The British again mentioned desire to increase their strength in cruisers from 50 to 70 ships.

Reports of the proposals came as surprise, both because Britain is even now awaiting reply from Japan on proposals made to her, and because the United States always has firmly refused to agree to lowered battleship and cruiser tonnage.

Its very buildings, nesting about the feet of its old State house on the hill, in the center of town, were built by or for Colonial stalwarts who built the nation.
